## Images and Preimages

A function $f:X\to Y$ acts on points, but it also acts on *subsets*. Pushing a
subset of $X$ forward gives its image, and pulling a subset of $Y$ back gives
its preimage. Preimages interact very well with set operations, which is why
they are the right tool in [[measure-theory]]: a [[measurable-function]] is
defined by the condition that preimages of measurable sets are measurable.

## Definitions

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a function.

:::{.definition data-title="Image and Preimage"}

The **image** of a subset $A\subseteq X$ is

$$
f(A) = \{f(x) : x\in A\} = \{y\in Y : \exists\,x\in A,\ f(x)=y\}.
$$

The **preimage** (or **inverse image**) of a subset $B\subseteq Y$ is

$$
f^{-1}(B) = \{x\in X : f(x)\in B\}.
$$

:::

The notation $f^{-1}(B)$ does not require $f$ to be invertible. Both
operations are maps between power sets,

$$
f:\mathcal{P}(X)\to\mathcal{P}(Y),
\qquad
f^{-1}:\mathcal{P}(Y)\to\mathcal{P}(X),
$$

and both are defined for every function. The **range** of $f$ is the image
$f(X)$, which can be strictly smaller than the codomain $Y$.

:::{.example data-title="Squaring"}

Let $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Then $f(\mathbb{R})=[0,\infty)$ and
$f([-2,1])=[0,4]$. For preimages, $f^{-1}([1,4])=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]$,
$f^{-1}(\{0\})=\{0\}$ and $f^{-1}((-\infty,0))=\emptyset$.

:::

## Properties of the Preimage

The preimage commutes with all set operations. For subsets $B,B_1,B_2\subseteq Y$
and a family $(B_i)_{i\in I}$ indexed by an arbitrary set $I$:

| Operation | Identity |
|:--|:--|
| Unions | $f^{-1}\left(\bigcup_i B_i\right)=\bigcup_i f^{-1}(B_i)$ |
| Intersections | $f^{-1}\left(\bigcap_i B_i\right)=\bigcap_i f^{-1}(B_i)$ |
| Complements | $f^{-1}(Y\setminus B)=X\setminus f^{-1}(B)$ |
| Differences | $f^{-1}(B_1\setminus B_2)=f^{-1}(B_1)\setminus f^{-1}(B_2)$ |
| Monotonicity | $B_1\subseteq B_2\implies f^{-1}(B_1)\subseteq f^{-1}(B_2)$ |
| Composition | $(g\circ f)^{-1}(C)=f^{-1}\left(g^{-1}(C)\right)$ |

:::{.proof}
The statement $x\in f^{-1}(B)$ means only that $f(x)\in B$, which is a
pointwise membership test, so it passes through any logical operation. For
example,

$$
x\in f^{-1}(B_1\cap B_2)
\iff f(x)\in B_1 \text{ and } f(x)\in B_2
\iff x\in f^{-1}(B_1)\cap f^{-1}(B_2),
$$

and the same argument works for unions, complements and differences.
:::

This is why preimages are used in measure theory. If $\mathcal{G}$ is a
$\sigma$-algebra on $Y$, then $\{f^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal{G}\}$ is a
$\sigma$-algebra on $X$, and this is why a random variable is defined by
the condition $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}$ (see [[random-variables]] and
[[generated-sigma-algebra]]).

## Properties of the Image

The image only partly commutes with set operations. For subsets
$A,A_1,A_2\subseteq X$ and a family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$:

| Operation | Relation |
|:--|:--|
| Unions | $f\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right)=\bigcup_i f(A_i)$ |
| Intersections | $f\left(\bigcap_i A_i\right)\subseteq\bigcap_i f(A_i)$ |
| Differences | $f(A_1)\setminus f(A_2)\subseteq f(A_1\setminus A_2)$ |
| Complements | $f(X)\setminus f(A)\subseteq f(X\setminus A)$ |
| Monotonicity | $A_1\subseteq A_2\implies f(A_1)\subseteq f(A_2)$ |
| Composition | $(g\circ f)(A)=g\left(f(A)\right)$ |

There is no general relation of the form $f(X\setminus A)=Y\setminus f(A)$.
One has $Y\setminus f(A)\subseteq f(X\setminus A)$ when $f$ is surjective,
and equality when $f$ is bijective.

**Why intersections fail.** Take $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $A_1=\{-1\}$ and
$A_2=\{1\}$. Then $A_1\cap A_2=\emptyset$, so $f(A_1\cap A_2)=\emptyset$, but
$f(A_1)\cap f(A_2)=\{1\}$. Two different points can collide in the image.

Equality is recovered exactly when $f$ is injective.

:::{.theorem data-title="Images and Injectivity"}

The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is injective;
2. $f(A_1\cap A_2)=f(A_1)\cap f(A_2)$ for all $A_1,A_2\subseteq X$;
3. $f(A_1\setminus A_2)=f(A_1)\setminus f(A_2)$ for all
   $A_1,A_2\subseteq X$.

:::

:::{.proof}
The inclusion $\subseteq$ in (2) and the inclusion $\supseteq$ in (3) hold for
every function. Suppose $f$ is injective. If $y\in f(A_1)\cap f(A_2)$, then
$y=f(a_1)=f(a_2)$ with $a_i\in A_i$, and injectivity gives $a_1=a_2\in
A_1\cap A_2$, which proves (2). If $y=f(a)$ with $a\in A_1\setminus A_2$ and
also $y\in f(A_2)$, then $y=f(a')$ with $a'\in A_2$ and $a=a'$, a
contradiction, so $y\notin f(A_2)$ and (3) holds.

Conversely, suppose $f$ is not injective, so $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ for some
$x_1\neq x_2$. With $A_1=\{x_1\}$ and $A_2=\{x_2\}$, we have
$f(A_1\cap A_2)=\emptyset\ne f(A_1)\cap f(A_2)$, so (2) fails, and
$f(A_1\setminus A_2)=f(A_1)\ne\emptyset=f(A_1)\setminus f(A_2)$, so (3) fails.
:::

## Interaction of Image and Preimage

For $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$,

$$
A\subseteq f^{-1}\big(f(A)\big),
\qquad
f\big(f^{-1}(B)\big)=B\cap f(X)\subseteq B.
$$

Moreover,

- $f^{-1}(f(A))=A$ for all $A\subseteq X$ if and only if $f$ is injective,
- $f(f^{-1}(B))=B$ for all $B\subseteq Y$ if and only if $f$ is surjective.

So injectivity and surjectivity are exactly the conditions under which $f$ and
$f^{-1}$, as maps between power sets, invert each other.

The pair also forms a **Galois connection**,

$$
f(A)\subseteq B \iff A\subseteq f^{-1}(B).
$$

This single equivalence encodes the two inclusions above: it means that $f$ is
the left adjoint of $f^{-1}$ on the power-set lattices. As a right adjoint, the
preimage preserves all intersections (limits), while the image, as a left
adjoint, preserves all unions (colimits).

Two more useful identities are

$$
f\big(A\cap f^{-1}(B)\big)=f(A)\cap B,
\qquad
f^{-1}(B)=\emptyset \iff B\cap f(X)=\emptyset.
$$

## Summary

| Operation | Preimage $f^{-1}$ | Image $f$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Unions | $=$ | $=$ |
| Intersections | $=$ | $\subseteq$ ($=$ iff injective) |
| Complements | $=$ (complement in the matching space) | no general equality |
| Differences | $=$ | $f(A_1)\setminus f(A_2)\subseteq f(A_1\setminus A_2)$ ($=$ iff injective) |

Preimages are well behaved with respect to all set operations, while images
are well behaved only with respect to unions.
